---
title: "Adverse event reporting in FAERS, 2004–2026"
subtitle: "A reproducible analysis of the complete FDA Adverse Event Reporting System corpus"
author: "Alexander Goncearenco"
date: last-modified
abstract: |
  This report analyses every adverse event report the FDA has published since 2004 — 20.3 million
  after deduplication, spanning both the legacy LAERS and current FAERS eras. It rebuilds and
  corrects an earlier exploratory analysis that worked from a 10,000-report sample drawn through
  the rate-limited openFDA API, and extends it to the questions that sample could not support:
  signal detection with shrinkage and multiplicity control, confounder adjustment, and the internal
  structure of a report. Every number is produced by a DVC pipeline from FDA's own published
  archives.
---

```{python}
# | label: setup
import json
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
from IPython.display import HTML, display

ROOT = Path("..")
RESULTS = ROOT / "results"
FIGURES = ROOT / "figures"


def load_json(name):
    return json.loads((RESULTS / name).read_text())


def desc(name):
    return pl.read_parquet(RESULTS / "descriptive" / f"{name}.parquet")


def fig(name, caption=""):
    """Embed the Vega-Lite spec so the chart stays interactive in the rendered site."""
    spec = (FIGURES / f"{name}.vl.json").read_text()
    html = (
        f'<div id="vis-{name}" class="vega-figure"></div>'
        "<script>vegaEmbed("
        f"'#vis-{name}', {spec}, "
        "{actions: {export: true, source: false, editor: false}}"
        ").catch(console.error);</script>"
    )
    if caption:
        html += f'<p class="figure-caption"><em>{caption}</em></p>'
    display(HTML(html))


dedup = load_json("dedup_stats.json")
norm = load_json("normalize_stats.json")
harm = load_json("harmonize_stats.json")["totals"]
sig = load_json("signals/summary.json")
fan = load_json("signals/fanout.json")
strat = load_json("stratify_summary.json")
manifest = load_json("source_manifest.json")


def n(x):
    return f"{int(x):,}"
```

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega@5"></script>

## What this is, and what it replaces

An adverse event report is a voluntary notification that something undesirable happened to someone
taking a medical product. It names the patient's drugs and the reactions observed. It does **not**
say which drug caused which reaction — that link is simply not recorded — and no report is
validated before it enters the database.

Everything below follows from that. These data can show that an event is reported *disproportionately
often* alongside a drug. They cannot show that the drug caused it, and they cannot estimate how often
it happens, because the number of people taking the drug without incident is unknown. Disproportionate
reporting is a signal to investigate, not a finding.

This analysis replaces a 2020 Jupyter notebook that explored the same database through the openFDA
web API. That notebook asked good questions and was candid about its limits: it could not compute
reactions per report, could not deduplicate, could not correct for the confounders it had itself
identified, and drew its record-level conclusions from a 10,000-report sample. The API made all four
impossible. Working instead from FDA's quarterly ASCII archives — 3.5 GB covering the whole corpus,
against 113 GB for the equivalent JSON — removes all four constraints.

::: {.callout-note}
## Provenance
`{python} n(manifest["n_quarters"])` quarterly archives, `{python} n(manifest["total_bytes"])` bytes,
2004Q1–2026Q2, each pinned by SHA-256. `{python} n(harm["DEMO"])` raw report records parsed into a
canonical schema spanning both the LAERS (2004Q1–2012Q3) and FAERS (2012Q4–) eras.
:::

## How much of the database is actually distinct

A case is resubmitted every time follow-up information arrives, and each submission appears in a
different quarterly file. Counting submissions therefore overcounts patients. Separately, FDA
publishes lists of cases it has withdrawn.

```{python}
# | label: tbl-dedup
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Step": [
            "Raw report records parsed",
            "Removed: FDA-retracted cases",
            "Removed: superseded case versions",
            "**Distinct cases analysed**",
        ],
        "Records": [
            n(dedup["records_raw"]),
            f'−{n(dedup["records_removed_as_retracted"])}',
            f'−{n(dedup["records_removed_as_superseded"])}',
            f'**{n(dedup["records_final"])}**',
        ],
    }
).to_pandas()
```

**`{python} f'{dedup["duplicate_fraction_of_raw"]:.1%}'` of the raw corpus is redundant.** The 2020
notebook saw the consequence of this without being able to name it: a block of "quite repetitive"
rows in its clustergram, which it guessed came from "duplicates in the database or other artifacts".
It did — 4.0 million superseded versions of cases counted again each time they were resubmitted.

`{python} n(dedup["cases_spanning_both_eras"])` cases were opened under LAERS and followed up under
FAERS. These only link because case identifiers survived the 2012Q4 transition; an analysis treating
the two eras as separate datasets would double-count every one of them.

One duplicate class remains: the same incident submitted independently by, say, a patient and their
physician, under different case ids. Detecting those needs probabilistic matching on demographics and
drug lists. It is not attempted here, so the corpus is *deduplicated*, not duplicate-free.

## The corpus, and who is in it

```{python}
# | label: fig-growth
fig("corpus_growth")
```

Reports grew roughly sevenfold, from `{python} n(desc("reports_per_year").filter(pl.col("year")==2004)["reports"][0])`
in 2004 to a peak near 1.57 million in 2021. 2026 is partial. Growth of this size over 22 years is
itself a confounder: a drug approved in 2022 is evaluated against a baseline dominated by reports
that predate it, which is why calendar period is adjusted for later.

```{python}
# | label: fig-sex
fig("sex_over_time")
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-age
fig("age_distribution")
```

Among reports recording a sex, `{python} f'{10719893/(10719893+7048525):.1%}'` are female — matching
the notebook's earlier estimate. The more consequential number is what is *missing*:
`{python} f'{8388236/dedup["records_final"]:.0%}'` of reports record no usable patient age at all.
Any age-stratified conclusion rests on the 59% that do, and that subset is not a random sample.

```{python}
# | label: fig-reporters
fig("reporters")
```

**Consumers now file more reports than physicians** — 8.88 million against 4.46 million. This is a
genuine change in the character of the database rather than a processing artifact, and it cuts
against the intuition that FAERS is primarily a clinician-reported system. Consumer reports carry
less clinical detail, which is part of why the missing-age fraction is so high.

fig("top_ingredients")

```{python}

```

Acetaminophen has displaced aspirin at the top since 2020. The leading *reactions* are worth reading
carefully: `DRUG INEFFECTIVE` (1.27M) and `OFF LABEL USE` (839k) outrank every clinical event. Neither
is an adverse reaction — they are reasons a report was filed. `DEATH` ranks third, and is an outcome
whose cause is unstated. The notebook flagged exactly this and it remains true: the most common terms
in the reaction field are substantially not reactions.

```{python}
# | label: fig-indications
fig("top_indications")
```

The single most common indication, by a factor of six, is `PRODUCT USED FOR UNKNOWN INDICATION`
(5.43M). Stratifying by indication — the obvious way to control for why a drug was prescribed — is
therefore unavailable for a quarter of the corpus.

## The structure of a report

```{python}
# | label: fig-structure
fig("report_structure")
```

The notebook could not compute this. It noted the API "does not allow analytics other than counting
reports with only one variable to group by", and concluded the data would have to be loaded into
Spark or a relational database first.

A report carries a mean of 3.18 drugs and 2.98 reactions, but a **median of one drug** — the mean is
pulled up by a long tail reaching 171 drugs and 456 reactions on a single report. That tail is why
the drug–event join has to be built carefully: the worst single report contributes 39,648 drug–event
pairs on its own, and the corpus generates `{python} n(fan["total_pairs"])` pairs in total.

This structure is also the reason no drug can be attributed a reaction. With three drugs and three
reactions on a report, all nine combinations are equally supported by the record.

### Dechallenge and rechallenge

Withdrawing a drug and seeing the reaction abate — then reintroducing it and seeing the reaction
return — is the strongest causal evidence a spontaneous report can carry. The notebook tried to
quantify how much of the database has it, estimated roughly 2% from marginal counts, and closed the
section noting "more data preprocessing needed".

Computed directly from the joint distribution, with missing values kept distinct from negative
outcomes:

```{python}
# | label: tbl-challenge
ch = desc("challenge_table")
tot = ch["drug_records"].sum()
val = ch.filter(
    pl.col("role_cod").is_in(["PS", "SS"]) & (pl.col("dechal") == "Y") & (pl.col("rechal") == "Y")
)
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Category": [
            "Drug records total",
            "Suspect drug, positive dechallenge AND positive rechallenge",
        ],
        "Records": [n(tot), n(val["drug_records"].sum())],
        "Share": ["100%", f'{val["drug_records"].sum()/tot:.3%}'],
    }
).to_pandas()
```

**0.147%**, not 2%. The earlier estimate was inflated by reading marginal counts as if the three
fields were independent; they are not. The practical consequence is stark: for roughly 1 drug record
in 680 does the database contain the validation protocol that would support a causal reading. The
rest is association.

## Which drug–event pairs report disproportionately

Every measure below is computed on a 2×2 table of *reports*, restricted to primary and secondary
suspect drugs, for pairs with at least 3 co-reports —
`{python} n(sig["n_pairs"])` pairs over `{python} n(sig["n_total_reports"])` reports.

Four screening rules are applied. All four are reported because none is authoritative, and their
disagreement is informative.

```{python}
# | label: fig-agreement
fig("signal_agreement")
```

```{python}
# | label: tbl-signals
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Rule": [
            "ROR₀₂₅ > 1 (reporting odds ratio)",
            "PRR ≥ 2, χ² ≥ 4 (MHRA)",
            "IC₀₂₅ > 0 (BCPNN, WHO-UMC)",
            "EB05 ≥ 2 (MGPS, FDA)",
            "Fisher exact, BH q < 0.05",
        ],
        "Pairs flagged": [
            n(sig["signals"]["signal_ror"]),
            n(sig["signals"]["signal_prr_mhra"]),
            n(sig["signals"]["signal_ic"]),
            n(sig["signals"]["signal_eb05"]),
            n(sig["signals"]["signal_fdr"]),
        ],
    }
).to_pandas()
```

Each rule screens on a **lower confidence or credible bound**, never a point estimate. This matters
more than it sounds: a reporting odds ratio of 8 computed from two co-reports is noise, and screening
on the raw ratio is the most common way to manufacture spurious signals. The 2020 notebook used the
lower bound for ROR and PRR, which was right, but evaluated it on two hand-picked pairs.

EB05 is the most conservative at `{python} n(sig["signals"]["signal_eb05"])` pairs, and is very nearly
a subset of the others: `{python} n(sig["concordant_all_four"])` pairs satisfy all four rules
simultaneously. That is the shrinkage doing its job.

```{python}
# | label: fig-shrinkage
fig("shrinkage_effect")
```

```{python}
# | label: tbl-gp
gp = sig["gamma_poisson"]
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Hyperparameter": ["α₁", "β₁", "α₂", "β₂", "w (mixture weight)", "Converged"],
        "Fitted value": [
            f'{gp["alpha1"]:.4f}',
            f'{gp["beta1"]:.4f}',
            f'{gp["alpha2"]:.4f}',
            f'{gp["beta2"]:.5f}',
            f'{gp["weight"]:.4f}',
            str(gp["converged"]),
        ],
    }
).to_pandas()
```

The gamma-Poisson mixture converged from multiple starting points. Points fall below the diagonal
precisely where evidence is thin — an extreme raw ratio from a handful of reports is pulled back
toward the null, while a ratio supported by thousands of reports is left alone.

### Does it recover what we already know?

A signal-detection pipeline that cannot rediscover established drug safety findings is not
trustworthy on novel ones. Nine associations that appear on approved product labelling, several as
boxed warnings, were checked blind against the output:

```{python}
# | label: tbl-controls
scored = pl.scan_parquet(RESULTS / "signals" / "scored.parquet")
controls = [
    ("METFORMIN HYDROCHLORIDE", "LACTIC ACIDOSIS"),
    ("AMIODARONE HYDROCHLORIDE", "PULMONARY TOXICITY"),
    ("ALLOPURINOL", "STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME"),
    ("CLOZAPINE", "AGRANULOCYTOSIS"),
    ("WARFARIN", "HAEMORRHAGE"),
    ("ATORVASTATIN CALCIUM", "RHABDOMYOLYSIS"),
    ("ISOTRETINOIN", "DEPRESSION"),
    ("HEPARIN SODIUM", "THROMBOCYTOPENIA"),
    ("LISINOPRIL", "COUGH"),
]
rows = []
for ing, pt in controls:
    r = scored.filter((pl.col("ingredient") == ing) & (pl.col("pt") == pt)).collect()
    if r.height:
        x = r.row(0, named=True)
        rows.append(
            {
                "Ingredient": ing.title(),
                "Reaction": pt.title(),
                "Co-reports": n(x["n_ij"]),
                "ROR₀₂₅": f'{x["ror025"]:.1f}',
                "EB05": f'{x["eb05"]:.1f}',
                "IC₀₂₅": f'{x["ic025"]:.2f}',
            }
        )
pl.DataFrame(rows).to_pandas()
```

All nine are flagged by every rule. Implausible pairings behave correctly in the other direction:
aspirin–alopecia returns EB05 = 0.19 and is not flagged.

### What ranks highest, and why that is a warning

The pairs with the largest EB05 in the whole corpus are **not** adverse reactions:

```{python}
# | label: tbl-top-signals
top = (
    scored.filter(pl.col("n_ij") >= 200)
    .sort("eb05", descending=True)
    .head(6)
    .select("ingredient", "pt", "n_ij", "eb05")
    .collect()
)
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Ingredient": [r["ingredient"].title() for r in top.to_dicts()],
        "Reaction term": [r["pt"].capitalize() for r in top.to_dicts()],
        "Co-reports": [n(r["n_ij"]) for r in top.to_dicts()],
        "EB05": [f'{r["eb05"]:,.0f}' for r in top.to_dicts()],
    }
).to_pandas()
```

A radioisotope tracer is *administered in order to* perform the scan whose abnormality is recorded.
Anosognosia — a patient's unawareness of their own illness — is a feature of the psychosis
zuclopenthixol treats, not a reaction to it. Raised prolactin is the expected pharmacology of a
dopamine antagonist. Further down the same ranking, "gadolinium deposition disease" names its own
cause. These are indication bias, expected pharmacology and tautology, ranked at the very top by
every measure — and they rank there precisely *because* the association is real and
near-deterministic.

This is the practical lesson of the whole exercise. Disproportionality finds strong statistical
association. Whether that association reflects harm, the reason for prescribing, or a naming
convention is not decidable from these data.

## Do signals survive confounder adjustment?

The notebook identified sex and age as likely confounders and could not act on it. Each is applied
here as a separate Mantel–Haenszel stratification, along with calendar period, on a random sample of
`{python} n(strat["by_variable"][0]["tested"])` signalling pairs.

```{python}
# | label: tbl-strat
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Adjustment": ["Sex", "Age band", "Calendar period (5y)"],
        "Pairs tested": [n(v["tested"]) for v in strat["by_variable"]],
        "Still signalling": [
            f'{n(v["surviving"])} ({v["survival_rate"]:.1%})' for v in strat["by_variable"]
        ],
        "Heterogeneous (Breslow–Day p<0.05)": [
            f'{n(v["heterogeneous"])} ({v["heterogeneous"]/v["tested"]:.0%})'
            for v in strat["by_variable"]
        ],
    }
).to_pandas()
```

The result is two-sided, and the second half matters more than the first.

**Adjustment removes almost nothing** — 98.5% to 100% of signals survive. Confounding by sex, age
or period is not what generates these associations.

**But homogeneity is rejected for half to three-quarters of them.** A pooled Mantel–Haenszel estimate
assumes one common odds ratio across strata; where Breslow–Day rejects that, the pooled number
averages genuinely different effects and is misleading on its own. The honest reading is that these
confounders do not *create* signals but do *modify* them, and a stratum-specific estimate should be
read instead of the pooled one.

One caveat stated plainly: at these sample sizes Breslow–Day has enormous power and will detect
heterogeneity too small to matter clinically. The test was calibrated against simulated data with a
known common odds ratio and showed a 6.8% rejection rate against a nominal 5%, so it is not simply
always rejecting — but the effect sizes, not the p-values, are what should drive interpretation.

```{python}
# | label: fig-strat
fig("stratified_survival")
```

## Reporting artefacts over time

```{python}
# | label: fig-trends
fig("reaction_trends")
```

The notebook compared raw yearly counts of Death, Pain and Dyspnoea and read the divergence as a
reporting bias. Raw counts rise with the corpus, so that comparison partly measured database growth.
Plotted as a share of each year's reports, the picture is different: what looked like a rising trend
in Death is substantially the database getting larger.

## Limitations

- **No causality, and no rates.** These are reporting associations. The denominator — people exposed
  without an event — is unknown, so incidence cannot be estimated.
- **MedDRA drift.** Preferred terms are treated as stable strings across 22 years, but MedDRA has
  been revised continuously and terms are renamed, split and merged. Some apparent temporal trend is
  vocabulary change. Correcting this needs the licensed MedDRA release, which cannot ship here.
- **No drug class hierarchy.** RxNorm→ATC mapping requires a UMLS licence. Cluster interpretation by
  pharmacologic class is therefore not attempted rather than approximated badly.
- **Drug resolution is 97.6%, not 100%.** `{python} f'{norm["resolution_counts"]["unresolved"]/norm["rows_out"]:.1%}'`
  of drug rows keep an unresolved free-text name. They fall below the minimum-support threshold and
  do not enter the signal tables, but they are absent from marginal counts.
- **Approximate q-values.** Benjamini–Hochberg assumes independence or positive dependence. Drug–event
  tests share reports and are dependent, so the stated FDR level is approximate.
- **Residual duplicates.** Independent submissions of the same incident under different case ids are
  not detected.
- **Partial dates.** Dates given as year or year-month are completed to the start of the period,
  biasing those toward January and month-starts.

## Reproducing this

```bash
git clone https://github.com/neksa/openfda-faers && cd openfda-faers
uv sync
dvc repro
```

No credentials and no cloud storage are needed: FDA hosts the source archives, `dvc.lock` pins every
intermediate by hash, and `results/source_manifest.json` records a SHA-256 for each of the
`{python} n(manifest["n_quarters"])` inputs. FDA republishes quarterly extracts as snapshots and can
revise them in place, so `faers verify` reports drift against those checksums rather than letting it
change the numbers silently.

Full run is roughly 25 minutes on a 10-core laptop, dominated by the download.
